To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the effect of unlabled data depends on the model that generates the training data, the model used to build the classifiers, and the amount of labeled data available for training.
unlabeled data may degrade the classification performance of a generative classifier when the classifier is based on an incorrect assumption about the data-generating process.

(a) generative classifiers are not robust to the addition of unlabeled data, and (b) generative classifiers perform better when the number of training data increases, and the number of unlabeled data is large.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: When should unlabeled data be used to improve classification performance?
the following question: How does the addition of unlabeled data to the training set affect the performance of a generative classifier?
the question: How does the use of unlabeled training examples affect the performance of a generative classifier?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effect of unlabled data is unpredictable and can be either positive or negative.
unlabeled data should not be included in a training set for a generative classifier unless the model used to build the generative classifier is the same model that generates the training data.

, in the case where the model used to generate data is different than the model used to build the classification system, the use of unlabeled data can actually degrade the performance of the classification system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
generative classifiers can be adversely affected by unlabeled data.
unlabeled training data are not necessarily beneficial to generative classifiers, and that the effect of unlabled data depends on the modeling assumptions used to construct the classifier.
unlabeled data should be added to the training set with caution, especially when there are modeling discrepancies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
unlabeled training data can degrade the classification performance of generative classifiers, and the degradation depends on the discrepancy between modeling assumptions and the underlying model.
the use of unlabeled data can be harmful if the modeling assumptions used to train the classifier are not appropriate.
unlabeled data should only be used to augment a pool of labeled data when there is strong evidence that the unlabeled data is generated by the same model that generated the labeled data.
